html:
The last of Rome's wars against the Celtiberians of inland Spain, fought around the hill town of Numantia on the upper Douro. After an earlier round of fighting in the 150s, war flared again in 143 BCE and dragged on for ten years.

Numantia was small, but Roman army after army failed against it. In 137 BCE the consul Gaius Hostilius Mancinus was trapped and had to surrender his army. A young officer, Tiberius Gracchus, arranged the terms. The Senate refused the treaty and handed Mancinus over to the Numantines, who sent him back.

In 134 BCE Rome sent Scipio Aemilianus, the man who had destroyed Carthage. He did not storm the town. He drilled his soldiers hard and ringed Numantia with walls, ditches and camps, then waited. After months of starvation the town surrendered in 133 BCE. Many defenders killed themselves; the rest were sold as slaves and the town was razed.

Both Gaius Marius and the African prince Jugurtha served under Scipio there. Numantia became a Spanish symbol of resistance to the end.
